opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important lesson from the last few years is that the Transformer didn't win only because it's expressive. It won because it fits the hardware extremely well. Attention is basically big matrix multiplications, highly parallel during training, and that matches what GPUs and tensor cores are good at. Older RNNs were arguably more elegant in some ways, but they were sequential, so they couldn't use the hardware efficiently, and they lost. So when we design new architectures, I don't think we can treat hardware efficiency as an afterthought. It has to be part of the design from day one.

That's a big motivation behind my work on linear attention and linear RNNs like DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. The goal isn't just lower asymptotic complexity on paper. Plenty of efficient-attention ideas had nice big-O numbers but were slower than FlashAttention in wall-clock time, because they were memory-bound or didn't use tensor cores. What matters is whether you can write the computation in a chunkwise, matmul-heavy form, so you get parallelism during training and a constant-size recurrent state during inference. In my view, an architecture that can't be written that way is unlikely to scale, however clever the math is.

I also think the relationship goes both ways. Hardware has been co-evolving with the Transformer: more tensor-core throughput, specialized support for low precision, and memory hierarchies tuned for attention-style workloads. But the bottlenecks are shifting. Training is mostly compute-bound, while inference, especially long-context inference and long reasoning traces, is increasingly limited by memory bandwidth and KV cache size. That's where fixed-state recurrent models, or hybrids that mix a few full-attention layers with many linear or state-space layers, become really attractive. I expect hybrid architectures to be the practical direction for the next generation. You keep some softmax attention for precise retrieval and use efficient recurrent layers for most of the sequence modeling.

There's also an expressivity question that I find exciting. Simple linear attention is quite weak, both in memory capacity and in the kinds of state tracking it can do. Things like the delta rule, gating, and allowing negative eigenvalues in the state transition make these models more powerful, closer to real RNNs, while keeping them parallelizable. So the research frontier, to me, is finding the most expressive recurrence that you can still compute efficiently with matrix multiplications. That's where algorithm design and hardware awareness really meet.

So my short answer is that the next generation of architectures should be designed jointly with the hardware: think about I/O, memory, and parallelism alongside modeling power. The architectures that win will be the ones that are both expressive and efficient on the chips we actually have, not just in theory.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware is tuned for attention-style workloads and that sequential RNNs could not use hardware efficiently, disadvantaging alternatives.

r002.rationale: It highlights inference efficiency, but does not say that lower training efficiency can be acceptable or that such an architecture can still find a market.

r003.rationale: It pairs lower asymptotic complexity in linear attention with chunkwise, matrix-multiplication-heavy computation.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention FlashAttention 4 or a shift in the bottleneck to exponential computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that Transformers won not because attention is the most elegant idea, but because it was the idea that mapped best onto the hardware we had. Matrix multiplication is what GPUs are good at, and attention turned sequence modeling into big dense matmuls that you can parallelize over the whole sequence at training time. RNNs lost largely because they couldn't do that. So in a sense the co-evolution has already happened once, and the lesson is that whatever comes next has to respect the hardware just as much.

The constraint that matters now is different from the one in 2017, though. Compute keeps growing much faster than memory bandwidth and memory capacity. On modern accelerators, the tensor cores are so fast that the bottleneck is usually moving data in and out of HBM, not doing arithmetic. That changes what you should optimize for. Standard attention has a KV cache that grows linearly with context length, so at inference time you're paying a memory and bandwidth cost on every single token that has nothing to do with how much thinking you actually need to do. That's why we've seen so much work on linear attention, state space models, and other forms of what I'd call recurrent models with a fixed-size state. They compress the context into a constant amount of memory, which is a much better fit for the bandwidth-bound regime.

But the key point is that it's not enough to have a good recurrent formulation in math. You need a parallel training algorithm that still runs as matmuls. A lot of our work on things like gated linear attention and the chunkwise algorithms is exactly about this: you split the sequence into chunks, do the intra-chunk computation as a dense matmul that the tensor cores love, and carry the state across chunks recurrently. That way you get the hardware efficiency of Transformers during training and the constant-memory efficiency of RNNs during inference. If you only have the first, you're a Transformer; if you only have the second, you're a 2015 LSTM and nobody will train you at scale.

So for the next generation, I'd say a few things. First, I don't think it's attention versus everything else. Hybrids are the practical answer for now, where you keep a few softmax attention layers for precise retrieval and use linear or state-based layers for the bulk of the sequence mixing. Full attention is very hard to beat on tasks that need exact lookup over a long context, and you shouldn't throw that away.

Second, architecture design should be done together with kernel design. You should ask, for every operator, how many bytes move per FLOP, whether it can be expressed as a matmul, how it behaves in the decode setting with batch size one. If you design the algorithm first and hope someone writes a fast kernel later, you usually end up with something that looks good in a paper and never ships.

And third, I think the more interesting frontier is making the recurrent state itself smarter. There's a whole line of work on treating the state as a fast weight that gets updated online, essentially doing a little bit of learning at test time, and people have shown you can do things like delta-rule updates in a way that's still hardware friendly. That's where I'd bet the architecture improvements come from: not a new attention variant, but a better way of deciding what to keep in a bounded memory, implemented so that it still saturates the tensor cores.

r001.rationale: The response says Transformers fit GPU matrix-multiplication hardware, while RNNs lost because they could not parallelize that way; it also stresses keeping recurrent methods compatible with tensor-core matmuls. This communicates the hardware advantage over alternatives.

r002.rationale: It describes recurrent models as a better fit for inference memory bandwidth, but says a parallel training algorithm is still necessary. It does not state that lower training efficiency can be acceptable when inference efficiency is the priority.

r003.rationale: The response recommends expressing operations as matmuls and discusses bytes moved per FLOP, but does not identify reducing FLOPs while retaining matmul computation as a design strategy.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention FlashAttention 4 or a shift in the performance bottleneck to exponential computation.

astra-6.text:
I think we should treat architecture and hardware as a joint design problem. An architecture can look very efficient on paper, but if it moves too much data or cannot use the hardware’s parallelism, that efficiency may never translate into lower latency or lower cost.

So I would start by asking where the bottleneck is. During training, you care about computation, memory, and communication across devices. During inference, especially when generating tokens one at a time, moving model weights and accessing the KV cache can become major constraints. The best architecture may differ depending on which workload you’re optimizing.

That opens up room to rethink attention, memory, and how we combine different kinds of layers. For example, you might use attention where access to individual past tokens is valuable, and a more compact state elsewhere. But the important test is whether that tradeoff preserves model quality while improving performance on real hardware—not just reducing the theoretical operation count.

And the co-evolution should go both ways. We shouldn’t constrain every new architecture to what today’s accelerators happen to do well. Hardware designers also need evidence about which new operations are useful and likely to scale. To me, the next generation comes from that feedback loop: design the model, build an efficient implementation, measure the actual bottlenecks, and let those measurements inform both the next architecture and the next hardware.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes training and inference bottlenecks, but does not state that a Linear Attention architecture could find a market despite lower training efficiency when inference efficiency is the priority.

r003.rationale: It mentions reducing theoretical operation count and rethinking attention, but does not identify reducing FLOPs while retaining matrix-multiplication-based computation as a design strategy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should treat hardware as part of the architecture design space from the beginning. A model can look very efficient in terms of FLOPs and still run slowly because it moves too much data, uses operations that are difficult to parallelize, or requires frequent communication between devices.

Transformers benefit from large matrix multiplications, which accelerators handle well. But attention also creates costs in memory and data movement, especially as the context grows. So the question is: can we change the computation so that we preserve the capabilities we care about while making better use of the hardware?

That means designing the architecture and its implementation together. For example, if we introduce sparsity, we need to ask whether the hardware can actually exploit that sparsity. If we compress the model’s state, we need to measure whether that reduces memory traffic without introducing another bottleneck. Theoretical efficiency is a starting point; actual training throughput and inference latency are the test.

And the influence should go both ways. We should adapt architectures to existing hardware, but also identify useful computational patterns that future hardware could support better. I don’t think that necessarily leads to one universal architecture. Different constraints—long-context processing, high-throughput training, or low-latency generation—may lead to different designs.
